fixes.explanation: Close, friend, but David says something much bigger. He says these men of violence "…stir up war all day long." (Psalm 140:2). Not once in a while, but all day long. I think that's why he's crying out to the LORD.
You've got it, baker. David says these men "…devise evil in their hearts and stir up war all day long." (Psalm 140:2). Not once in a while, but all day long. I think that's a heavy thing to read.
Yes, snakes. David says they "…sharpen their tongues like snakes…" (Psalm 140:3). Then he adds that the venom of vipers is on their lips. A sharp tongue with venom on it is a hard picture.

A lion's a good guess, since it's a famous fierce animal. But David picks a different animal: "They sharpen their tongues like snakes; the venom of vipers is on their lips." (Psalm 140:3). Snakes it is, and the venom of vipers is part of the picture.

That's the one. These men of violence "…scheme to make me stumble." (Psalm 140:4). To scheme means it's planned, not an accident. I think David feels like somebody is out to trip him up, and he takes that straight to the LORD.

Right on the money, baker. David says, "The proud hide a snare for me; the cords of their net are spread along the path, and lures are set out for me." (Psalm 140:5). That's a trap on the very path he walks. Somebody did some serious planning.

Stones would be a rough walk, friend, but David doesn't mention any. He says, "The proud hide a snare for me; the cords of their net are spread along the path…" (Psalm 140:5). It's a snare and a net. The snare is hidden, and the net is spread along the path.

True, baker. With a snare hidden and a net spread along his path, David says to the LORD, "You are my God." (Psalm 140:6). Then he adds, "Hear, O LORD, my cry for help." Even with all that along his path, he talks to the LORD anyway.

Not quite, friend. David does say it, and he says it with traps set along his path. He says to the LORD, "You are my God." (Psalm 140:6). Then he asks, "Hear, O LORD, my cry for help." I'd say that's some real faith under pressure.

That's exactly it. David prays, "May the heads of those who surround me be covered in the trouble their lips have caused." (Psalm 140:9). The trouble is what he asks to cover their heads. It's trouble their own lips have caused.

Wandering doesn't fit this ending, baker. David says, "Surely the righteous will praise Your name; the upright will dwell in Your presence." (Psalm 140:13). Dwell means to stay and live there. That's the opposite of wandering.
